summary:
PARALLAX is an open pipeline and web tool that finds objects that really move in NASA SPHEREx infrared images, rejects false "movers", and measures how far away they are. A hidden planet like Planet Nine would appear as one faint dot that shifts between images taken six months apart — but most changes between two SPHEREx images are fake: each image is taken at a different infrared wavelength, bright objects leave optical ghosts, and stars never subtract perfectly.

We built fair image pairing (same-wavelength comparisons with a trust badge), difference imaging, automatic detection, track linking that rejects static stars, ghosts and glare, and a parallax-plus-orbit distance fit. We tested it blind on real SPHEREx data: without being told where Neptune is, the pipeline found it in 64 of 74 image differences and measured 29.93 AU, versus 29.89 AU from NASA JPL Horizons (0.13% error), used only for grading. We also found that SPHEREx's own OUTLIER/TRANSIENT flags mark moving objects, so the usual mask discards real movers. A machine-learning classifier (ROC AUC 0.96 on real candidates), a volunteer review page and an interactive Parallax Lab make the method usable and teachable for everyone.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

PARALLAX turns raw NASA SPHEREx Level 2 images into an answer to "is something here moving, and how far away is it?" — and shows the method so anyone can understand and check it.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Fair pairs (Honest Blink): SPHEREx images each pixel at a slightly different infrared wavelength, so we only compare images taken at almost the same wavelength; every pair carries a trust badge.

2. Difference imaging: each science image minus a reference image of the same sky taken at another time, reprojected onto the same grid, with zodiacal light removed and noise from the VARIANCE layer.

3. Detection: new sources above 5 sigma whose light was not in the reference.

4. Linking and rejection: detections from different exposures are joined into tracks; static sources, optical ghosts (fixed detector offset from a bright mover) and glare companions are rejected automatically.

5. Distance: a circular-orbit parallax model fitted from the June track to the December track.

6. Machine learning: a gradient-boosting real/bogus classifier on 14 features per candidate (ROC AUC 0.96 on 405 real SPHEREx candidates with grouped cross-validation, versus 0.56 when ranking by brightness alone). A "Help review" page lets volunteers check uncertain candidates; their answers become new training labels.

RESULTS ON REAL DATA (blind test on Neptune)

The detector, linking and distance fit never read the ephemeris; JPL Horizons is used only to grade. Neptune was found in 64 of 74 image differences, it was the only track classed as a real mover, 8 fake tracks were rejected, and the distance came out 29.93 AU versus 29.89 AU (0.13%). Keeping SPHEREx's OUTLIER/TRANSIENT flags, which mark moving sources, recovered 10 detections that a standard mask removes. Injection tests show one image finds sources down to about 1/500 of Neptune's brightness.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Researchers: an open, tested pipeline, a mover-aware flag policy, and a measured detection depth.

- Citizen scientists: fair image pairs and a review page with practice and feedback.

- Students and the public: the Parallax Lab — a live simulator, a "find the hidden planet" game, and the real Neptune measurement computed in the browser.

HONEST LIMITS AND NEXT STEPS

We claim no discovery: Neptune validates the method. The Neptune cutouts were chosen around its position, and Neptune's orbit is nearly circular. A Planet-Nine-like object is far fainter than one SPHEREx image can show, so the next step is Shift & Stack (adding many images along each trial path), then Uranus as a second blind object and an open-sky search.

TOOLS

Python (NumPy, Astropy, reproject, SciPy, pandas, scikit-learn, Matplotlib), TypeScript, React and Vite, Vercel hosting, GitHub. Data from NASA/IPAC IRSA (SPHEREx DR1 and QR3) and JPL Horizons. All code is open: https://github.com/aknur3289-spec/nasa-spherex
